questions.q: A survey shows that& $73 %$ of the persons working in an office like coffee, whereas~$65 %$ like tea. If~$x$ denotes the percentage of them, who like both coffee and tea, then~$x$ cannot be:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$n\left(C\right) = 73, n \left(T\right) = 65, n \left($C ∩ T\right) = x$,~

Considering that value of~n\left($C ∪ T\right)$~cannot exceed~$100$~in terms of percentage, we get

n\left($C ∪ T\right) ≤ 100$

$⇒ $n\left($C\right) + $n\left($T\right) - $n \left(C ∩ T\right) ≤ 100$

$⇒ x ≥ 38$

Therefore,~$x \ne 36$.

$n\left(C ∩ T\right)$\lemin\$lleft(n\left($C\right), $n\left($T\right)\right) ⇒ x ≤ 65$

$⇒ 38 ≤ x ≤ 65$

Hence~$x$~may assume values~$63, 54, 38$.

questions.q: Let $R$ be a relation on $Z \times Z$ defined by $( a, b ) R ( c, d )$ if and only if $ad - bc$ is divisible by $5$ . Then $R$ is
options: Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
Reflexive but neither symmetric not transitive
Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given relation $R: \left(a, b\right)R \left($c, d\right)$

And $ad - bc = 5k \left\{\text{where}k \in Z\right\}$

Now, for reflexive $R: \left(a, b\right)R\left(a, b\right)$

$⇒ ab - ba = 0$ which is divisible by $5$

So, the relation is reflexive,

Now, for symmetric $R: \left(c, d\right)R \left($a, b\right)$

$⇒bc - ad = - 5k$ which is divisible by $5$

So, the relation is symmetric,

Now for transitive relation, $R: \left($a, b\right)R \left(c, d\right)R \left($e, f\right)$

Taking example \left($a, b\right) ≡ \left(1, 2\right), \left(c, d\right) ≡ \left(10, 10\right), \left(e, f\right) ≡ \left(4, 4\right)$

Now, $ad - bc = 10 - 20 = - 10$

$cf - ed = 40 - 40 = 0$

But $af - be = 8 - 4 = 4$ which is not divisible by $5,

Hence, the relation is reflexive, symmetric but not transitive.

$

questions.solution:

questions.q: Out of all the patients in a hospital $89 %$ are found to be suffering from heart ailment and $98 %$ are suffering from lungs infection. If $K %$ of them are suffering from both ailments, then $K$ can not belong to the set:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $H$~and $L$~is set of people suffered from heart ailment and lungs infections respectively.

$n\left(H\right) = 89 %$

$n\left(L\right) = 98 %$

$n \left(H ∩ L\right) = K %$

$max \left\{n ( H ) , n \left($L\right)\right\} $\$len\left(H ∪ L\right)$\len \left($U\right)$

Where,~$U$~is the universal set.

$⇒ 98 $\len\left($H ∪ L\right) ≤ 100$

$⇒ 98 $\len\left($H\right) + $n\left($L\right) - $n\left($H ∩ L\right) ≤ 100$

$⇒ 98 ≤ 89 + 98 - k ≤ 100$

$⇒ 0 ≤ 89 - k ≤ 2$

$⇒ - 89 $\le -$k $\le -$87$

$⇒ 87 ≤ K ≤ 89$

questions.q: Let $R$ be a relation on $N \times N$ defined by \left(a, b\right)R  \left(c, d\right)$~ if and only if $ad \left(b - c\right) = bc  \left(a - d\right)$. Then $R$ is$
options: symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
transitive but neither reflexive nor symmetric
reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,& \left(a, b\right)R \left(c, d\right) ⇒ ad \left($b - c\right) = $bc\left($a - d\right)$

$⇒ \left($a, b\right)R\left(c, d\right) ⇔ \dfrac{b - c}{bc} = \dfrac{a - d}{ad}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{c} - \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{1}{d} - \dfrac{1}{a}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{1}{d} - \dfrac{1}{c}$

Reflexive:

\left(a, b\right)R\left(a, b\right) ⇒ \dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{1}{b} - \dfrac{1}{a}$

It is false. So, given relation is not reflexive.

Symmetric:

\left(a, b\$right)R\left($c, d\right) ⇒ $\dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{1}{d} - \dfrac{1}{c}

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{c} - \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{1}{b} - \dfrac{1}{a}

$∴ \left($c, d\right)R \left(a, b\right)$

It is symmetric.

Transitive:

\left(a, b\right)R\left(c, d\right) ⇒ \dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{1}{d} - \dfrac{1}{c}$

\left(c, d\right)R\left(e, f\right) = \dfrac{1}{c} - \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{1}{e} - \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{1}{e} - \dfrac{1}{f}$

$⇒ \left(a, b\right) R \left($e, f\right)

So, not transitive.

$

questions.q: Let $A = \left\{2, 3, 4\right\}$ and $B = \left\{8, 9, 12\right\}$. Then the number of elements in the relation $R = \left\{\left(\left({a}_{1}, {b}_{1}\right), \left({a}_{2}, {b}_{2}\right)\right) \in \left(A \times B, A \times B\right): {a}_{1}\text{divides}{b}_{2}\text{and}{a}_{2}\text{divides}{b}_{1}\right\}$& is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$A = \left\{2, 3, 4\right\}, B = \left\{8, 9, 12\right\}$

And~${a}_{1} \in A, {b}_{2} \in B$

Now finding elements where~${a}_{1}$ divides~${b}_{2}$~we get,

\left({a}_{1}, {b}_{2}\right) \in \left\{\left(2, 8\right), \left(2, 12\right), \left(3, 9\right), \left(3, 12\right), \left(4, 8\right), \left(4, 12\right)\right\}$

Also given,~${a}_{2} \in A, {b}_{1} \in B$

Now finding elements when~${a}_{2}$ divides~${b}_{1}$, we get,

\left({a}_{2}, {b}_{1}\right) \in \left\{\left(2, 8\right), \left(2, 12\right), \left(3, 9\right), \left(3, 12\right), \left(4, 8\right), \left(4, 12\right)\right\}$

Hence, Number of relations~$= 6 \times 6 = 36$

questions.q: Let ${R}_{1} = \left\{\left(a, b\right) \in N \times N: \left|a - b\right| \le 13\right\}$~and ${R}_{2} = \left\{\left(a, b\right) \in N \times N: \left|a - b\right| \ne 13\right\}$~Then on $N$:
options: ${R}_{1}$~is an equivalence relation but ${R}_{2}$& is not
${R}_{2}$~is an equivalence relation but ${R}_{1}$& is not
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
To check if ${R}_{1}$~is transitive -

Let~$a = 16, b = 4, c = 1$

Here \left|a - b\right| = \left|16 - 4\right| \le 13$~holds true

now~\left|b - c\right| = \left|4 - 1\right| \le 13$~$⇒ \left|3\right| ⩽ 13$~ ~also holds true

but~\left|a - c\right| = \left|16 - 1\right| ≰ 13$

Hence~${R}_{1}$~is not transitive

Similarly, to check transitivity of~${R}_{2}$

Let~$a = 16, b = 4, c = 3$

Here~\left|a - b\right| = \left|16 - 4\right| \ne 13\text{and}\left|b - c\right| = \left|4 - 3\right| \ne 13$

but~\left|a - c\right| = \left|16 - 3\right| = 13$

Hence,~${R}_{2}$~is also not transitive.

Hence neither~${R}_{1}$~nor~${R}_{2}$ \text{ and } is an equivalence relation

$

questions.q: Let $\mathrm{A}=\{1,2,3, \ldots, 10\}$ and R be a relation on A such that $\mathrm{R}=\{(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}): \mathrm{a}=2 \mathrm{~b}+1\}$. Let  \left(\mathrm{a}_1, \mathrm{a}_2\right)$, \left(a_2, a_3\right),  \left(a_3, a_4\right), \ldots .,\left(a_k, a_{k+1}\right)$ be a sequence of $k$ elements of R such that the second entry of an ordered pair is equal to the first entry of the next ordered pair. Then the largest integer k , for which such a sequence exists, is equal to :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{a}=2 \mathrm{~b}+1 \\ & 2 \mathrm{~b}=\mathrm{a}-1 \\ & \mathrm{R}=\{(3,1),(5,2), \ldots,(99,49)\}
\end{aligned}$
Let $(2 m+1, m),(2 \lambda-1, \lambda)$ are such ordered pairs.
According to the condition
$\mathrm{m}=2 \lambda-1 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~m}=\text { odd number }$
$\Rightarrow 1^{\text {st }}$ element of ordered pair $(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b})$
$a=2(2 \lambda-1)+1=4 \lambda-1$
Hence $a \in\{3,7, \ldots, 99\}$
$\Rightarrow \lambda \in\{1,2, \ldots, 25\}$
\Rightarrow set of sequence
$\begin{aligned} & \left\{(4 \lambda-1,2 \lambda-1),(2 \lambda-1, \lambda-1),\left(\lambda-1, \frac{\lambda-2}{2}\right), \ldots \ldots .\right\} \\ & 2^{\text {nd }} \text { element of each ordered pair }=\frac{\lambda-2^{\mathrm{r}-2}}{2^{\mathrm{r}-2}}\end{aligned}$
For maximum number of ordered pairs in such sequence
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{\lambda-2^{\mathrm{r}-2}}{2^{\mathrm{r}-2}}=1 \text { or } 2 ; 1 \leq \lambda \leq 25 \\ & \lambda=2^{\mathrm{r}-1} \text { or } \lambda=3.2^{\mathrm{r}-2}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & \text { Case-I : } \lambda=2 \mathrm{r}-1 \\ & \lambda=2,2^2, 2^3, 2^4 \\ & r=2,3,4,5\end{aligned}$
Hence maximum value of $r$ is 5 when $\lambda=16$
$\begin{aligned} & \text { Case-II }: \lambda=3.2^{\mathrm{r}-2} \\ & \lambda=3,6,12,24 \\ & \mathrm{r}=2, \quad 3, \quad 4,5\end{aligned}$
Hence maximum value of $r$ is 5 when $\lambda=24$

questions.q: Let $N$ be the set of natural numbers and a relation~$R$ on $N$ be defined by $R = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in N \times N: x^{3} - 3x^{2}y - xy^{2} + 3y^{3} = 0\right\}$.~Then the relation $R$ is
options: symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$x^{3} - 3x^{2}y - xy^{2} + 3y^{3} = 0$

$⇒ x\left(x^{2} - y^{2}\right) - 3y\left(x^{2} - y^{2}\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(x - 3y\right)\left(x - y\right)\left(x + y\right) = 0$

Now, $x = y ∀ \left(x, y\right) \in N \times N$ so~its a reflexive relation.
But not symmetric & transitive

Since, \left(3, 1\right)$ satisfies but \left(1, 3\right)$ does not.

Also \left(3, 1\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 1\right)$~satisfies but \left(3, - 1\right)$ does not.

questions.q: The relation $R=\{(x, y): x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $x+y$ is even $\}$ is:
options: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For reflexive $(x, x) \in \mathbb{R}, x \in \mathbb{Z}\Rightarrow x+x=2 x \rightarrow \text { even }$
For symmetric of $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}$ then $(y, x) \in \mathbb{R}$ when $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}x+y \rightarrow$ even
$\Rightarrow y+x \rightarrow \text { even }$
for transitive if $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R} \Rightarrow x+y \rightarrow$ even
$(y, z) \in \mathbb{R} \Rightarrow y+z \rightarrow \text { even }x+2 y+z \rightarrow$ even
$\Rightarrow x+z$ is even
$\Rightarrow(x, z) \in \mathbb{R}\Rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is an equivalence relation.

questions.q: The number of relations, on the set&  \left\{1, 2, 3\right\}$~containing~\left(1, 2\right)$~and~  \left(2, 3\right)$ \text{ and } which are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, is _________.$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

Set& $A = \left\{1, 2, 3\right\}$

Now Cartesian product~$A \times A = \left\{\left(1, 1\right), \left(2, 1\right), \left(1, 2\right), . . . . . . . . , \left(3, 3\right)\right\}$

Now, given the relation is reflexive,

So,~\left(1, 1\right), \left(2, 2\right), \left(3, 3\right) \in R$

Also given \left(1, 2\right), \left(2, 3\right) \in \mathbb{R}, \left(1, 3\right)$~must~$\in R$

Now finding,~Possible cases :

Case-1: All of~\left(2, 1\right), \left(3, 2\right), \left(3, 1\right) \notin R \to 1$~relation.

Case-2: Only one of~\left(2, 1\right), \left(3, 2\right), \left(3, 1\right) \in \mathbb{R} \to 3$~relations.

For example if relation is~\left\${\left($1, 1\right), \left($2, 2\right), \left($3, 3\right), \left($2, 1\right)\right\}$~then it is reflexive as well as transitive as~ \left(2, 2\right), \left(2, 1\right) \to \left(2, 1\right)\text{is present in relation}$

Note that exactly two of~\left(2, 1\right), \left(3, 2\right), \left(3, 1\right) \in R$~is~not possible because if two of these~$\in R$,~third must~$\in R$ to make relation transitive.

Total number of relations~$= 4$

questions.q: Let $X = \left\{n \in N: 1 \le n \le 50\right\}$. If $A = \left\{n \in X: nisamultipleof2\right\}$ and $B = \left\{n \in X: nisamultipleof7\right\}$, then the number of elements in the smallest subset of $X$, containing both $A$ and $B$, is.

questions.solution:
Here,& $A = \left\{2, 4, 6, . . . . 50\right\}$~and~$B = \left\{7, 14, . . . 49\right\}$

Required smallest subset is~$A ∪ B$.

So,~$n \left(A ∪ B\right) = n \left($A\right) + $n\left($B\right) - $n\left($A ∩ B\right)$
$= 25 + 7 - 3$
$= 29$.
